name: Possible beer in a Late Uruk jug at Godin Tepe
summary: A spot test of yellow deposits in an incised Godin Tepe jug gave an oxalate result consistent with beer, among other possibilities.
description: Michel, McGovern and Badler interpreted yellow deposits inside a double-handled jug at Godin Tepe, in Iran’s central Zagros, as probable beer residue. Oxalate and the jar’s form support their interpretation, but the spot test and marker lack specificity. Barley from the period’s botanical assemblage made it a plausible ingredient.

impact.note: Catalogue scope is the reported beer interpretation of one Godin Tepe vessel. Reach, depth and later effects remain unverified.

date.label: ca. 3500–2900 BCE, original Period V assignment
date.basis: Context range used by Michel and colleagues for Period V. It is the original report’s broad context chronology.

events.statement: A Feigl test gave a positive oxalate result for pale interior deposits sampled from the crisscross grooves of a double-handled jug in the Period V Oval complex. The original investigators interpreted this as evidence consistent with beer.

evidence.supports: Provides the contextual period range, sherd description, result and comparison controls.

evidence.locator: Direct Evidence for Prehistoric Fermented Beverages
evidence.supports: Independently explains why the method and marker do not securely identify beer.

events.caveats: No direct date or independently specific beer marker is available for the tested deposits.

earliest_record.rationale: Dates the archaeological context of the reported discovery. The identification of beer remains tentative.

unresolved.note: Check the Royal Ontario Museum specimen and excavation lot against the residue-sampled sherd, then seek independently replicated residue identification with appropriate controls.
A similar double-handled sherd, GOT_20, is of a local fabric. This does not locate the production of its contents or establish how the shape or brewing knowledge travelled.

evidence.supports: Independent provenance analysis of the same vessel type.

research.note: The fuller 1993 original report gives an earlier-to-later Period V range and attributes barley only from archaeological context. A later provenance study does not support treating the assemblage as straightforward evidence of imported Uruk ceramics.

caveats: The chemical result does not securely identify beer, barley or local brewing. A sherd of the same vessel type tested in a separate provenance study had a local clay signature. It has not been matched to the residue-tested vessel.
